title: Neuter nouns: gifts, words, war
subtitle: Lesson 8 · Neuter nouns: -um, plural -a
intro: Until now every noun was either feminine (*puella*) or masculine (*servus*). Latin has a third gender, **neuter** ('neither'), for many things and ideas: *bellum* 'war', *dōnum* 'gift', *verbum* 'word', *oppidum* 'town', *caelum* 'sky'. Neuter nouns have one simple trick: the subject and the object look the same. You also get *novus* 'new' and the very common verb 'give': *dat* 'he / she gives', *dant* 'they give'.

example.en: The men do not love war.

vocab.notes: *dōnum* 'gift' (compare 'donate'). One gift *dōnum*, several gifts *dōna*, as subject or object.

example.en: The boy has a new gift.
The girl looks at the new words.

vocab.notes: *oppidum* is a town, smaller than a city. Plural *oppida* 'towns'.
*caelum* 'sky, heaven' (compare 'celestial'). Usually used in the singular.
*dat* 'he / she gives', *dant* 'they give'. One of the 30 commonest Latin words (compare 'donor', 'data' = 'things given').

grammar.title: Neuter nouns: -um, plural -a
grammar.body:
Neuter nouns end in **-um** in the singular and **-a** in the plural, and the **same form works as subject and object**: *Bellum longum est* 'The war is long' and *Virī bellum nōn amant* 'The men do not love war.' Plural: *Dōna multa sunt* 'There are many gifts', *Dominus dōna dat* 'The master gives gifts.'

So how do you tell who does what? Look at the other word and the verb: in *Puer dōnum habet* only *puer* can be the subject, so *dōnum* is the thing he has.

Adjectives describing a neuter noun take the same endings: *dōnum novum* 'a new gift', *dōna nova* 'new gifts', *oppida parva* 'small towns'. Careful: plural *-a* is not the *-a* of *puella*.

examples.en: The boy has a new gift.
The men do not love war.

examples.la: Oppidum parvum est, sed caelum māgnum est.
examples.en: The town is small, but the sky is big.

reading.title: Oppidum novum
reading.la: Oppidum parvum et novum est, et caelum māgnum est. Sextus dominus bonus est. Bellum nōn amat; dōna amat. Nunc servī dōna multa portant, et Sextus dōna dat. Mārcus puer equum novum habet et rīdet. Iūlia quoque dōnum habet. Virī verba bona narrant et dominum laudant. Puerī et puellae caelum spectant et semper rīdent.
reading.en: The town is small and new, and the sky is big. Sextus is a good master. He does not love war; he loves gifts. Now the slaves carry many gifts, and Sextus gives the gifts. Marcus, a boy, has a new horse and laughs. Julia also has a gift. The men say good words and praise the master. The boys and girls look at the sky and keep laughing.
reading.hint: Neuter words look the same as subject and object: find *oppidum*, *caelum*, *bellum*, *dōna*, *dōnum* and *verba*, and ask each time who is doing what.
